column1: What is the core visual invariant governing where a viewer's eye looks first on a displayed model?
column2: The eye always seeks the highest contrast edge first (the silhouette), then travels along lines of implied motion toward the next point of resolution.

column1: Why does silhouette quality matter more than interior detail for display models viewed at distance?
column2: The outer boundary (silhouette) is processed by the visual cortex before color or surface detail; a weak, blobby silhouette fails at three meters regardless of interior detail quality.

column1: Define 'sight line' and state the typical angle range for a standing adult viewer at a standard display table.
column2: A sight line is the imaginary ray from a viewer's eye to a point on the model. At ~165cm eye height viewing a 75cm table, the primary sight line is approximately 15–25 degrees below horizontal, steepening when closer and flattening toward horizontal at greater distance.

column1: What is the first invariant of display structural engineering regarding friction-fit connections?
column2: Never rely on friction alone for sustained structural loads — stud-on-stud clamping force (4–6 N per stud) diminishes over months under sustained vertical shear due to ABS creep.

column1: What is ABS creep and why does temperature matter for displayed LEGO models?
column2: ABS is viscoelastic and deforms slowly over time under constant sub-yield load (creep). Creep rate accelerates with temperature, so models near windows or heat sources show more joint relaxation than those in climate-controlled rooms.

column1: What is the difference between designing a model for construction versus for display?
column2: Construction handling distributes load dynamically through the hands; display subjects the model to gravity as a static, unrelenting force on every pin/axle/stud joint continuously for months or years, requiring different structural solutions (not just rotational stiffness via bracing).

column1: What perceptual principle underlies successful LEGO display environments with multiple models?
column2: Visual coherence through constrained variance — consistent baseline parameters (palette, style, texture) combined with controlled variation (focal hierarchy, asymmetry) to avoid monotony or chaos.

column1: What is the 'Planck-length equivalent' of LEGO construction space, and why does it matter for scale mixing?
column2: The 1×1 brick (8mm × 8mm × 9.6mm) quantizes all spatial relationships into integer multiples, making continuous scaling impossible; mixing minifigure scale (~1:48) with microscale (~1:192–1:350) elements causes perceptual dissonance and destroys immersion.

column1: What is the 'perceptual attention budget' in exhibition design?
column2: The finite cognitive/temporal resources a visitor brings to viewing, involving pre-attentive filtering (200–500ms) followed by focused attention (1.5–3s per fixation); exhibitions must balance stimulation to avoid fatigue or disengagement.

column1: How does the inverse-square law constrain luminaire placement in exhibition lighting?
column2: Illuminance falls off with the square of distance from a point source; doubling distance quarters illuminance. A spotlight at 30cm delivers 16× the illuminance of the same fixture at 120cm.

column1: Describe the compound lighting architecture recommended for revealing LEGO model form.
column2: Key lights at 30–45° elevation for primary shadows; fill lights at lower intensity to keep contrast ratios below 8:1 (avoiding detail crushing); rim/backlights at grazing angles (5–15° from horizontal) to separate subject from background.

column1: What causes the internal 'glow' effect seen in trans-clear/trans-colored LEGO elements under lighting?
column2: Subsurface scattering — photons penetrate 1–3mm into the translucent polymer matrix before re-emerging at adjacent surface points, creating a characteristic internal glow.
